Northern pike (Esox lucius) hatching occurs after an incubation period of approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days] when eggs are maintained at a spawning temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], a thermal condition typical of early spring in boreal lakes. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae measure about 0.875 centimeters [Lb = about 0.875 centimeters] in total length, a size that allows them to remain relatively inconspicuous among submerged vegetation during the lecithotrophic phase. This initial length is modest compared to other esocids of similar egg size, reflecting the species' strategy of producing numerous small offspring.

As the yolk-sac larva completes its endotrophic development and transitions to exogenous feeding, the juvenile fish embarks on a rapid growth trajectory that can eventually lead to a maximum recorded length of 150 centimeters [Li = 150 centimeters] in productive northern waters. Such ultimate total lengths are attained only in the most favorable habitats, where prey fish such as yellow perch and cyprinids are abundant. Interestingly, under the cooler thermal regimes characteristic of subarctic lakes (roughly 12 °C [T = 12 °C]), pike exhibit a remarkably long lifespan, with the oldest documented individuals reaching 20 years [am = 20 years] before succumbing to senescence.

The pubertal transition in this species is marked by both length and mass thresholds. Field surveys indicate that gonad maturation typically begins when individuals reach a total length of approximately 50.8 centimeters [Lp = approximately 50.8 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a wet weight of about 908 grams [Wwp = about 908 grams] in most populations. This onset of reproductive maturity, however, is not solely size-dependent; water temperature plays a critical role in regulating the timing of first reproduction. For pike inhabiting lakes where summer temperatures hover around 12 °C [T = 12 °C], first spawning events are typically observed at an age of 3 years after hatching [tR = 3 years after hatching], a delayed maturation that allows sufficient somatic growth to support the energetic demands of egg production.

Maximum reproductive output in northern pike is substantial, though heavily modulated by thermal conditions during the prespawning period. An individual female deposits approximately 274 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 274 eggs per spawning event], and completes approximately 365 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawning events per year], yielding a daily reproduction rate that is high but sustained only briefly during the spring spawning window. The eggs themselves are small and adhesive, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.0048 grams [Wwb = 0.0048 grams], a minimal maternal investment per offspring that is partially offset by high fecundity.

The maximum body mass recorded for adult northern pike in large, prey-rich water bodies can reach 24,600 grams [Wwi = 24,600 grams], a size class typically dominated by females that have outlived most conspecifics. These exceptionally large individuals are rare and are usually found in systems with low fishing pressure and abundant forage fish. The energetic surplus from favorable feeding conditions appears to allow a few individuals to exceed the 20-year longevity mark (20 years) [am = 20 years] when water temperatures remain moderate, though most pike in exploited populations seldom reach such an advanced age or massive size at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C].
